subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Structure 1.4–1.5 — counting particles by mass; ideal gases
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: The mole as a count of named particles
Relative atomic and formula mass on the carbon-12 scale
Molar mass and the n = m/M relationship
Empirical and molecular formulae from composition
Molar concentration, n = CV and unit conversions
Avogadro's law and reacting gas volumes
The assumptions of the ideal gas model
Where real gases depart from the model, and why
Molar volume and the relationships between p, V and T
Using PV = nRT and the combined gas law

questions.q: How many electrons are there in 0.200 mol of ammonia, NH₃? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; atomic numbers: H 1, N 7)
optionWhy: A student who stops at n × N_A counts molecules: 0.200 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²³ NH₃ molecules. Each molecule contains 10 electrons, so there are 1.20 × 10²⁴ electrons.

A student who counts only the electrons in a Lewis formula uses 5 + 3 = 8 valence electrons: 0.200 × 8 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.63 × 10²³. Nitrogen also has two 1s electrons; the molecule has 10 electrons in total.
One NH₃ molecule contains 7 + 3 × 1 = 10 electrons. Electrons = 0.200 × 10 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴.
A student who applies the ratio of 10 electrons per molecule the wrong way round divides: 1.20 × 10²³ ÷ 10 = 1.20 × 10²². There are more electrons than molecules, so multiply by 10: 1.20 × 10²⁴.
questions.explain: One NH₃ molecule contains 7 + 3 × 1 = 10 electrons. Electrons = 0.200 × 10 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴.
questions.working: Electrons per NH₃ molecule = Z(N) + 3 × Z(H) = 7 + 3 = 10. N(electrons) = 0.200 mol × 10 × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 1.204 × 10²⁴ ≈ 1.20 × 10²⁴.

questions.q: What is the relative formula mass, M_r, of hydrated calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂·4H₂O? (A_r: H 1.01, N 14.01, O 16.00, Ca 40.08)
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the water of crystallisation calculates 40.08 + 2(14.01 + 3 × 16.00) = 164.10. The four H₂O molecules are part of the formula unit: add 4 × 18.02 = 72.08 to give 236.18.
Add every atom, including the four water molecules: 40.08 + 2(14.01 + 3 × 16.00) + 4(2 × 1.01 + 16.00) = 40.08 + 124.02 + 72.08 = 236.18. M_r has no unit.
A student who lets the 2 after the bracket multiply only the O₃ counts 1 N and 6 O: 40.08 + 14.01 + 6 × 16.00 + 72.08 = 222.17. The 2 multiplies the whole NO₃ group, 2 N and 6 O: M_r = 236.18.

A student who treats the 4 like a coefficient in an equation counts one water molecule: 164.10 + 18.02 = 182.12. The 4 is part of the formula: each formula unit contains four H₂O, so add 4 × 18.02 = 72.08 to give 236.18.
questions.explain: Add every atom, including the four water molecules: 40.08 + 2(14.01 + 3 × 16.00) + 4(2 × 1.01 + 16.00) = 40.08 + 124.02 + 72.08 = 236.18. M_r has no unit.

questions.q: How many ions are there in 5.55 g of calcium chloride, CaCl₂? (N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹; A_r: Cl 35.45, Ca 40.08)
optionWhy: M(CaCl₂) = 40.08 + 2 × 35.45 = 110.98 g mol⁻¹; n = 5.55 ÷ 110.98 = 0.0500 mol. Each formula unit contains 3 ions (one Ca²⁺, two Cl⁻): 0.0500 × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²².
A student who stops at n × N_A counts formula units: 0.0500 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.01 × 10²². Each formula unit of CaCl₂ contains three ions, so there are 9.03 × 10²² ions.

A student who reads the Cl₂ in CaCl₂ as one unit counts two ions per formula unit: 0.0500 × 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²². CaCl₂ is a lattice of Ca²⁺ and separate Cl⁻ ions, three ions per formula unit.
A student who inverts n = m/M calculates 110.98 ÷ 5.55 = 20.0 'mol', giving 20.0 × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 3.61 × 10²⁵. The amount is mass ÷ molar mass: 5.55 ÷ 110.98 = 0.0500 mol.
questions.explain: M(CaCl₂) = 40.08 + 2 × 35.45 = 110.98 g mol⁻¹; n = 5.55 ÷ 110.98 = 0.0500 mol. Each formula unit contains 3 ions (one Ca²⁺, two Cl⁻): 0.0500 × 3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 9.03 × 10²².

questions.q: An oxide of iron contains 69.94% iron and 30.06% oxygen by mass. Which ratio of iron atoms to oxygen atoms gives its empirical formula? (A_r: O 16.00, Fe 55.85)
optionWhy: A student who rounds the ratio 1 : 1.50 to the nearest whole number gets 1 : 2. A value of 1.50 is not scatter: it means the whole-number ratio is 2 : 3.
A student who inverts n = m/M divides A_r by the percentage: 55.85 ÷ 69.94 = 0.799 and 16.00 ÷ 30.06 = 0.532, a ratio of 1.50 : 1, i.e. 3 : 2. The amount is mass ÷ A_r, which gives 2 : 3.
A student who takes the percentages as the ratio of atoms gets 69.94 : 30.06 = 2.33 : 1, i.e. 7 : 3. Iron atoms are much heavier than oxygen atoms, so each percentage must first be divided by A_r.
n(Fe) = 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252; n(O) = 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879. Dividing by 1.252 gives 1 : 1.50, and multiplying by 2 gives 2 : 3, so the empirical formula is Fe₂O₃.
questions.explain: n(Fe) = 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252; n(O) = 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879. Dividing by 1.252 gives 1 : 1.50, and multiplying by 2 gives 2 : 3, so the empirical formula is Fe₂O₃.
questions.working: n(Fe) = 69.94 ÷ 55.85 = 1.252 mol; n(O) = 30.06 ÷ 16.00 = 1.879 mol (per 100 g). Divide by the smaller: Fe 1.00, O 1.879 ÷ 1.252 = 1.50. Multiply by 2: Fe : O = 2 : 3, so the empirical formula is Fe₂O₃.

questions.q: A hydrocarbon contains 88.80% carbon and 11.20% hydrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 54.10 g mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula? (A_r: H 1.01, C 12.01)
optionWhy: A student who stops at the empirical formula picks C₂H₃. Its formula mass is 27.05, half the molar mass of 54.10 g mol⁻¹, so each molecule contains two C₂H₃ units: C₄H₆.
n(C) = 88.80 ÷ 12.01 = 7.394; n(H) = 11.20 ÷ 1.01 = 11.09; ratio 1 : 1.50, so the empirical formula is C₂H₃ (27.05). x = 54.10 ÷ 27.05 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₄H₆.

A student who rounds the ratio 1 : 1.50 down to 1 : 1 takes the empirical formula as CH (13.02); 54.10 ÷ 13.02 = 4.16 ≈ 4 gives C₄H₄. The ratio 1 : 1.50 must be doubled to 2 : 3, giving C₂H₃ and then C₄H₆. The misfit 4.16 is itself a warning.
A student who multiplies only the atom next to the bracket in (C₂H₃)₂ gets C₂H₆. The multiplier applies to the whole empirical unit: (C₂H₃)₂ = C₄H₆.
questions.explain: n(C) = 88.80 ÷ 12.01 = 7.394; n(H) = 11.20 ÷ 1.01 = 11.09; ratio 1 : 1.50, so the empirical formula is C₂H₃ (27.05). x = 54.10 ÷ 27.05 = 2, so the molecular formula is C₄H₆.
questions.working: Per 100 g: n(C) = 88.80 ÷ 12.01 = 7.394 mol; n(H) = 11.20 ÷ 1.01 = 11.09 mol. Ratio H : C = 11.09 ÷ 7.394 = 1.50, so C : H = 1 : 1.50 = 2 : 3 and the empirical formula is C₂H₃. Empirical formula mass = 2(12.01) + 3(1.01) = 27.05. x = 54.10 ÷ 27.05 = 2.00. Molecular formula = (C₂H₃)₂ = C₄H₆.

questions.q: A solution of chlorine in water contains 4.00 g of dissolved chlorine, Cl₂, per dm³. Ignore any reaction of chlorine with water. What is [Cl₂]? (A_r: Cl 35.45)
optionWhy: A student who uses A_r of chlorine as the molar mass of chlorine gas calculates 4.00 ÷ 35.45 = 0.113 mol dm⁻³. Dissolved chlorine is Cl₂, M = 70.90 g mol⁻¹, giving 0.0564 mol dm⁻³.
A student who multiplies by the molar mass calculates 4.00 × 70.90 = 284. Units show the error: g dm⁻³ × g mol⁻¹ is not mol dm⁻³. Divide: 4.00 ÷ 70.90 = 0.0564 mol dm⁻³.
A student who treats grams and moles as interchangeable changes only the unit. 4.00 g of Cl₂ is 4.00 ÷ 70.90 = 0.0564 mol, so [Cl₂] = 0.0564 mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: At the same temperature and pressure, a flask holds 0.640 g of oxygen, O₂, when filled with oxygen and 1.28 g of gas X when filled with X. What is the molar mass of X? (A_r: O 16.00)
optionWhy: A student who uses A_r of oxygen as the molar mass of oxygen gas gets n = 0.640 ÷ 16.00 = 0.0400 mol and M(X) = 1.28 ÷ 0.0400 = 32.0 g mol⁻¹. Oxygen gas is O₂, M = 32.00 g mol⁻¹.

A student who applies the mass ratio the wrong way round calculates 32.00 × 0.640 ÷ 1.28 = 16.0 g mol⁻¹. X gives the heavier sample with the same number of molecules, so M(X) = 32.00 × 1.28 ÷ 0.640 = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.
Equal volumes at the same T and p contain equal amounts: n = 0.640 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol. M(X) = 1.28 g ÷ 0.0200 mol = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.

A student who treats a mass in grams as an amount in moles takes n(X) = n(O₂) = 0.640 mol and calculates 1.28 ÷ 0.640 = 2.00 g mol⁻¹. 0.640 g of O₂ is 0.640 ÷ 32.00 = 0.0200 mol, so M(X) = 1.28 ÷ 0.0200 = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.
questions.explain: Equal volumes at the same T and p contain equal amounts: n = 0.640 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol. M(X) = 1.28 g ÷ 0.0200 mol = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.
questions.working: Same flask, same T and p, so by Avogadro's law n(X) = n(O₂) = 0.640 g ÷ 32.00 g mol⁻¹ = 0.0200 mol. M(X) = 1.28 g ÷ 0.0200 mol = 64.0 g mol⁻¹.

questions.q: According to the ideal gas model, what causes the pressure that a gas exerts on the walls of its container?
options: Moving particles collide with the walls and exert a force on them.
The particles repel one another, so they push outwards on the walls.
The weight of the particles presses on the container, mainly on its base.
The particles expand to fill the container and press against its walls.
optionWhy: In the model the particles move randomly and collide elastically with the walls. Each collision exerts a force on the wall; the pressure is the total force per unit area from these collisions, so it acts equally on every wall.

A student who pictures gas particles pushing each other apart picks this. The ideal gas model has no intermolecular forces, attractive or repulsive; the pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls as they move.

A student who links pressure to weight, as for a solid resting on a surface, picks this. Gas pressure acts equally in all directions, including upwards on a lid; it comes from particle collisions with the walls, not from the weight of the gas.

A student who gives the particles the properties of the bulk gas picks this. Particles do not change size; a gas fills its container because its particles move freely through the empty space, and the pressure comes from their collisions with the walls.
questions.explain: In the model the particles move randomly and collide elastically with the walls. Each collision exerts a force on the wall; the pressure is the total force per unit area from these collisions, so it acts equally on every wall.

questions.q: A sample of methane, CH₄, is kept at 300 K, first at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and then at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. It is a gas at both pressures. At which pressure does it deviate more from ideal gas behaviour, and why?
options: At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles collide more often and lose kinetic energy each time
At 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa, as its particles are close enough for their volume and attractions to matter
At 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, as its particles expand to fill the much larger volume of the gas
Neither, as at 300 K its particles move at the same average speed at both pressures
optionWhy: A student who thinks every collision loses kinetic energy picks this. Collisions are elastic in the model and, for a real gas at 300 K, the average kinetic energy of the particles is set by the temperature, which is the same at both pressures. The deviation at high pressure comes from the particles' own volume and the attractions between them.

At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas, and the attractions between them become significant. The ideal gas model ignores both, so methane deviates more at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

A student who thinks particles swell to fill their container picks this. Particles do not change size. At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their volume and the attractions between them are negligible and the gas behaves almost ideally.

A student who thinks deviation depends only on how fast the particles move (and so only on temperature) picks this. The average speed is indeed the same at both pressures, but at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa the particles are much closer together, so their own volume and the attractions between them become significant.
questions.explain: At high pressure the particles are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas, and the attractions between them become significant. The ideal gas model ignores both, so methane deviates more at 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Real gases deviate most at low temperature and high pressure.

questions.q: The graph shows PV / nRT plotted against pressure for a real gas at constant temperature, together with the line for an ideal gas. Which statement explains the behaviour of the real gas at the point marked A?
options: Attractions between the molecules pull them closer together, so the gas occupies a smaller volume than an ideal gas would.
The covalent bonds within each molecule are strong, and these bonds hold the neighbouring molecules close together.
The molecules have a volume of their own, so the gas is squeezed into less space than the ideal model predicts.
The molecules lose kinetic energy in their frequent collisions, so they strike the walls with less force than ideal particles.
optionWhy: The ideal model assumes no intermolecular forces. In a real gas the attractions between molecules reduce the volume (or the pressure on the walls) below the ideal value, so PV/nRT < 1 at A. At higher pressure (B) the molecules’ own volume dominates and the curve rises above the line.

Covalent bonds act within a molecule and have no effect on how molecules attract one another. The dip at A is caused by the intermolecular attractions (van der Waals forces) between molecules, which the ideal model ignores.

The molecules’ own volume acts the other way: it makes the gas harder to compress, so PV/nRT rises above 1 (the region around B). The dip at A comes from the attractions between molecules, which draw them closer together.

Collisions do not drain kinetic energy from a gas; at constant temperature the average kinetic energy is unchanged. The lower value of PV/nRT at A is due to attractions between the molecules, not to slower molecules.
questions.explain: The ideal model assumes no intermolecular forces. In a real gas the attractions between molecules reduce the volume (or the pressure on the walls) below the ideal value, so PV/nRT < 1 at A. At higher pressure (B) the molecules’ own volume dominates and the curve rises above the line.

questions.q: At STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa), 1.00 mol of helium (M = 4.00 g mol⁻¹) occupies 22.7 dm³. What volume does 1.00 mol of xenon (M = 131.29 g mol⁻¹) occupy at STP, if both behave as ideal gases?
options: 22.7 dm³, as heavy xenon atoms move at the same speed as the helium atoms
22.7 dm³, as volume depends only on the amount of gas at a given T and p
More than 22.7 dm³, as its much larger atoms take up more of the space
Less than 22.7 dm³, as a denser gas has its particles closer together
optionWhy: A student who thinks all particles move at the same speed at a given temperature picks this. At the same temperature the particles have the same average kinetic energy, so the heavier xenon atoms move much more slowly than helium atoms. The xenon sample occupies 22.7 dm³ because volume depends only on the amount of gas, not because the speeds are equal.

In an ideal gas the particles have negligible volume and exert no intermolecular forces, so at a given temperature and pressure the volume depends only on the amount of gas, not on the identity or mass of the particles. 1.00 mol of xenon at STP occupies the same 22.7 dm³ as 1.00 mol of helium.

A student who thinks bigger or heavier particles need more room picks this. The particles' own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas, so the size of the xenon atoms does not affect the molar volume: 1.00 mol of xenon occupies 22.7 dm³, the same as 1.00 mol of helium.

A student who explains density by particle spacing picks this: xenon is far denser than helium, so its atoms seem to be packed more closely. At the same temperature and pressure equal amounts of ideal gases occupy equal volumes, so the spacing is the same; xenon is denser because each of its atoms has a much larger mass.
questions.explain: In an ideal gas the particles have negligible volume and exert no intermolecular forces, so at a given temperature and pressure the volume depends only on the amount of gas, not on the identity or mass of the particles. 1.00 mol of xenon at STP occupies the same 22.7 dm³ as 1.00 mol of helium.
questions.working: Both samples are at the same temperature (273 K) and pressure (100 kPa) and contain the same amount of gas (1.00 mol). For an ideal gas V = nRT/p, which does not contain the molar mass, so V(Xe) = V(He) = 1.00 mol × 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ = 22.7 dm³.

questions.q: What volume does 72.0 g of oxygen gas, O₂, occupy at STP (273.15 K, 100 kPa)? Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP = 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹; A_r(O) = 16.00.
optionWhy: A student who uses 16.00 g mol⁻¹, the molar mass of oxygen atoms, gets n = 72.0 ÷ 16.00 = 4.50 mol and V = 4.50 × 22.7 = 102 dm³. Oxygen gas consists of O₂ molecules, so M = 32.00 g mol⁻¹.
A student who multiplies the mass by the molar volume gets 72.0 × 22.7 = 1634 dm³. The molar volume is the volume per mole, so the mass must first be converted to amount: n = 72.0 ÷ 32.00 = 2.25 mol.
A student who divides the molar volume by the amount gets 22.7 ÷ 2.25 = 10.1 dm³. The volume is the amount multiplied by the volume per mole: V = n × V_m = 2.25 × 22.7 = 51.1 dm³.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, the pressure, p, is plotted on the y-axis against 1/V on the x-axis, where V is the volume. Which description of the graph is correct?
options: A straight line with a negative gradient, as p falls as 1/V rises
A curve that falls and levels off, as p and V are inversely related
A straight line through the origin, as p doubles whenever V is halved
A horizontal line, as the particles' speed and hence p do not change
optionWhy: A student who thinks an inverse relationship is always a falling straight line picks this. p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: as 1/V rises p rises, giving a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient.

A student who expects every inverse relationship to look like a falling curve picks this without reading the x-axis. The falling curve is the graph of p against V. Plotting against 1/V turns the inverse relationship into a direct one: a straight line through the origin.

At constant temperature p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: halving V doubles 1/V and doubles p. A graph of p against 1/V is therefore a straight line through the origin.

A student who thinks pressure depends only on how fast the particles move picks this. At constant temperature the average speed is unchanged, but in a smaller volume the particles hit the walls more often, so the pressure rises as V falls.
questions.explain: At constant temperature p is inversely proportional to V, so p is directly proportional to 1/V: halving V doubles 1/V and doubles p. A graph of p against 1/V is therefore a straight line through the origin.

questions.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas in a gas syringe is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 40 °C. What happens to its volume?
options: It rises by about 7%, since its temperature in K does
It doubles, since 20 °C to 40 °C doubles its temperature
It increases, since each gas particle expands when heated
It stays the same, since the gas still fills the same syringe
optionWhy: At constant pressure V is proportional to absolute temperature. 20 °C = 293 K and 40 °C = 313 K, so V₂/V₁ = 313/293 = 1.07: the absolute temperature and the volume both rise by about 7%.

A student who treats Celsius temperature as proportional to volume picks this. 0 °C is not absolute zero, so doubling the Celsius temperature does not double the absolute temperature: 293 K to 313 K is a rise of only about 7%.

A student who thinks particles swell when heated picks this. The volume does increase, but not because the particles grow: they move faster, so to keep the pressure constant the gas must occupy more space. The increase is a factor of 313/293.
A student who thinks a gas always has the volume of its container picks this. The plunger of a gas syringe moves, so at constant pressure the gas expands as it is heated: V₂/V₁ = 313/293.
questions.explain: At constant pressure V is proportional to absolute temperature. 20 °C = 293 K and 40 °C = 313 K, so V₂/V₁ = 313/293 = 1.07: the absolute temperature and the volume both rise by about 7%.

questions.q: The graph shows the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant pressure plotted against temperature in °C. Measurements were made between 27 °C and 227 °C and the line is extrapolated back to the temperature axis. At what temperature would the volume of the gas be 48.0 cm³?
optionWhy: 227 × 48.0/40.0 treats volume as proportional to the Celsius temperature, which would put zero volume at 0 °C. The graph shows zero volume at −273 °C, so work in kelvin: 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K = 327 °C.

500 × 40.0/48.0 = 417 K puts the volume ratio the wrong way round, giving a lower temperature for a larger volume. The graph shows volume rising with temperature: T = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K = 327 °C.
The line reaches zero volume at −273 °C, so V is proportional to the kelvin temperature. V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C (500 K), so V = 48.0 cm³ at 500 × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K, which is 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
600 is the temperature in kelvin. The question asks in °C, so subtract 273: 600 K = 327 °C.
questions.explain: The line reaches zero volume at −273 °C, so V is proportional to the kelvin temperature. V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C (500 K), so V = 48.0 cm³ at 500 × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K, which is 600 − 273 = 327 °C.
questions.working: From the graph, V = 40.0 cm³ at 227 °C and the line extrapolates to V = 0 at −273 °C, so V ∝ T/K. T₁ = 227 + 273 = 500 K. T₂ = T₁ × V₂/V₁ = 500 K × 48.0/40.0 = 600 K; t₂ = 600 − 273 = 327 °C.

questions.q: A fixed mass of an ideal gas occupies 2.00 × 10⁻³ m³ at 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and 27 °C. It is compressed to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and at the same time its temperature rises to 87 °C. What is its new pressure?
optionWhy: A student who uses the Celsius temperatures gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 87/27 = 1.29 × 10⁶ Pa. The combined gas law needs absolute temperatures: 300 K and 360 K.
A student who inverts the temperature ratio gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 300/360 = 3.33 × 10⁵ Pa, as if heating lowered the pressure. From P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁).
T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K. P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa. The compression and the heating both raise the pressure.

A student who applies only the pressure–volume relationship gets 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 = 4.00 × 10⁵ Pa, ignoring the rise in temperature. Both variables changed, so the factor T₂/T₁ = 360/300 must be included.
questions.explain: T₁ = 300 K and T₂ = 360 K. P₂ = P₁ × (V₁/V₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 1.00 × 10⁵ × 4.00 × 1.20 = 4.80 × 10⁵ Pa. The compression and the heating both raise the pressure.
